issues.legal_issue: A person who is not a party to a written transaction may challenge it as sham and adduce evidence that its apparent terms were not intended to be acted upon.
material_facts: The occupants were not parties to the registered lease between the owners and the tenant.
The occupants alleged that the lease was a sham arrangement intended to avoid rent-control protections, rather than seeking to vary or contradict its written terms.
issues.conclusion: The occupants were permitted to plead that the lease was sham and to adduce evidence in support; the rules governing proof of the written terms did not bar that challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 did not apply because the occupants were not parties to the lease and were not seeking to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from its terms. A party may challenge the apparent validity of a document by alleging that the transaction it records was fictitious or not intended to be acted upon, but bears the burden of proving that allegation.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.challenger_is_not_party_to_document: The person challenging a written transaction was not a party to that document.
predicates.challenge_alleges_transaction_was_sham: The challenger alleges that the transaction recorded in the document was not genuine or was not intended to be acted upon.

issues.definition: When a person who is not a party to a document alleges in a rent-control eviction proceeding that the recorded transaction was sham, evidence may be considered to assess that allegation.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that a written transaction is sham must be proved by evidence supporting an irresistible inference, rather than conjecture or surmise.
material_facts: The occupants relied on testimony from witnesses whose evidence did not establish facts supporting the alleged rent-collection agency arrangement.
One witness did not address the premises in dispute, and other testimony was affected by the witnesses' own litigation with the tenant.
The tenant, who could have been a key witness, did not testify.
The available evidence did not displace the written lease and the competing testimony remained largely oath against oath.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the lease was sham; the arrangement was found to be genuine on the evidence and record in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The party alleging a sham transaction bears the burden of proof. Where direct evidence is unavailable, an inference may be drawn from circumstances, but the circumstances must support an irresistible inference and not merely conjecture or surmise.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.sham_transaction_alleged: A party alleges that a written transaction was not genuine or was not intended to be acted upon.
predicates.evidence_does_not_support_irresistible_i: The evidence and surrounding circumstances do not support an irresistible inference that the transaction was sham.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, an allegation of a sham transaction is not established when the evidence does not support an irresistible inference that the transaction was not genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising limited revisional jurisdiction cannot reverse a factual finding by re-evaluating the evidence without a sufficient basis to do so.
material_facts: The Appellate Authority found no weighty or material circumstances that displaced the written lease and directed eviction.
The High Court re-evaluated the evidence, drew different factual inferences, and treated the lease as sham.
The evidence before the High Court did not support the conclusion that the lease was sham.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the Appellate Authority's factual finding in its limited revisional jurisdiction, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: In a rent-control revision, the High Court's limited revisional jurisdiction did not justify re-evaluating the evidence and reversing the Appellate Authority's finding of fact on the record presented in this case.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision arising from a rent-control eviction decision.
predicates.lower_appellate_authority_made_factual_f: The lower appellate authority made a factual finding after evaluating the evidence.
predicates.revision_court_reverses_by_reweighing_ev: The revisional court reverses that finding by re-evaluating the evidence without a sufficient basis for doing so.

issues.definition: A revisional court's reversal is not justified when it reweighs evidence to overturn a factual finding without a sufficient basis.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant's transfer of possession or subletting without the landlord's written consent establishes a ground for eviction, and oral consent cannot replace the required written consent.
material_facts: The lease prohibited the tenant from subletting any part of the premises.
The tenant placed the occupants in possession of cabins and gave them rights to use those cabins under written occupation agreements.
The landlord's written consent to subletting was not present.
The High Court relied on alleged oral consent when rejecting this ground for eviction.
issues.conclusion: The ground for eviction based on unauthorized subletting was established, and the High Court could not substitute oral consent for written consent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 provides a ground for eviction where a tenant transfers rights under the lease or sublets the building or a portion of it without the landlord's written consent. Where the law requires written consent, oral consent does not satisfy that requirement.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_places_others_in_possession_of_pr: The tenant places other persons in possession of the premises or a portion of them.
predicates.landlord_written_consent_absent: The landlord has not given written consent to that placement or subletting.

issues.definition: When a tenant places others in possession in a rent-control eviction case without the landlord's written consent, the unauthorized-subletting ground for eviction is established.

issues.legal_issue: Constructing separate cabins within a hall that materially impairs the building's value or utility establishes a ground for eviction.
material_facts: The premises were a hall.
Several cabins were constructed in the hall so that they could be used as independent office premises.
The construction materially impaired the value or utility of the building.
issues.conclusion: The ground for eviction based on material impairment of the building's value or utility was established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 provides a ground for eviction where the tenant has made an act that materially impairs the value or utility of the building. The construction of several cabins in a hall, enabling their independent use as office premises, met that standard on these facts.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_makes_structural_changes: The tenant makes structural changes to the building or a portion of it.
predicates.changes_materially_impair_building_value: The changes materially impair the building's value or utility.

issues.definition: Structural changes that materially impair a building's value or utility establish the material-impairment ground for eviction in a rent-control eviction case.

issues.legal_issue: An application to amend pleadings must specifically identify the proposed omissions, alterations, substitutions, or additions.
material_facts: The occupants' applications gave only a vague description of the intended amendments.
Each application attached a wholly new written statement for substitution without specifying how the original pleading was to be changed.
The trial proceeded on the amended pleadings, but the occupants failed on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The applications did not satisfy the requirements for a properly specified amendment. Because the trial had proceeded on the amended pleadings and the occupants had failed on the merits, the Court left the matter at that.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion to permit amendments needed to determine the real questions in controversy; Section 153 provides a general power to amend proceedings; and Order 8 Rule 9 governs subsequent pleadings. An amendment applicant must specify exactly what is to be omitted, altered, substituted, or added so the court can assess the proposed change and its effect. The Court also referred to Order 6 Rule 18 concerning the time for making an allowed amendment, Order 6 Rule 7 concerning inconsistent new grounds, and the local amendment requiring the specific proposed changes to be stated. It observed that reasons for seeking amendment and any delay should be stated. The Court cited Bikram Singh v. Ram Baboo for the recognized concept of consequential amendments.

predicates.pleading_amendment_request: A party asks a court for permission to amend a pleading.
predicates.proposed_changes_not_specifically_identi: The request does not specify the precise omissions, alterations, substitutions, or additions proposed to the original pleading.

issues.definition: A request to amend a pleading is procedurally inadequate when it does not specifically identify the proposed changes.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment made in response to an opponent's amended pleading must be confined to answering that amendment and cannot introduce an unrelated new plea.
material_facts: The Court addressed the scope of a party's amendment after the opposing party had been allowed to amend its pleading.
The Court distinguished a responsive consequential amendment from an independent or primary amendment introducing a new plea.
issues.conclusion: A consequential amendment must answer the amendment permitted to the opposing party; a new plea cannot be introduced under the guise of a consequential amendment, although it may be sought by an independent amendment application.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs amendment of pleadings, and Order 6 Rule 7 prohibits raising a new ground of claim or an allegation inconsistent with prior pleadings except by amendment. In Bikram Singh v. Ram Baboo, the Court recognized the expression 'consequential amendment.' A consequential amendment must respond to the amendment allowed to the opposite party and cannot be used to introduce an unrelated new plea.

predicates.opponent_is_allowed_to_amend_pleading: The opposing party has been permitted to amend its pleading.
predicates.party_seeks_consequential_amendment: A party seeks to amend its pleading as a consequence of the opposing party's amendment.
predicates.proposed_plea_does_not_answer_opponent_a: The proposed plea does not answer the changes made in the opposing party's amended pleading.

issues.definition: A proposed plea that does not answer the opponent's amended pleading cannot be added as a consequential amendment.
